name: Apache Calcite
summary: A Java framework with everything a database needs to understand a query (SQL parser, validator, relational algebra and a rule-based, cost-based optimizer) but no storage of its own, which Hive, Flink, Druid, Dremio, Beam and many other systems embed as their SQL front end and planner.
intro: Calcite takes SQL text, parses it, checks it against a schema, and turns it into a tree of relational operators: scan, filter, project, join, aggregate and so on. Its optimizer then rewrites that tree with rules. Calcite ships hundreds of them, plus two planner engines to fire them: a cost-based one modeled on Volcano, which keeps sets of equivalent plans and picks the cheapest, and a cheaper one that fires rules, without costing them, until the plan stops changing. Physical properties such as sort order and partitioning are “traits” of an operator, and so is the calling convention, the system that will run it. That lets one plan span engines: a filter can be pushed into Splunk while the join with a MySQL table runs elsewhere.

On purpose, Calcite leaves out data storage, the algorithms that process data and a metadata repository. You bring those through adapters. An adapter tells Calcite which collections count as tables and can add rules that push work into its backend; the project includes adapters for JDBC databases, Cassandra, MongoDB, Elasticsearch, Druid, Kafka, Redis, Arrow, Spark, CSV and plain Java objects. What can’t be pushed down runs in Calcite’s own `Enumerable` operators, which iterate over rows in generated Java code. Most users never see Calcite directly: Hive uses it for cost-based optimization, Flink to parse and optimize batch and streaming SQL, Druid to parse and plan Druid SQL, and Dremio, Beam, Drill, Kylin, Feldera and Alibaba’s MaxCompute for parsing or planning. It also has a JDBC driver, built on its Avatica subproject, so an application can query any mix of adapters as one database. The latest release is 1.42.0 (31 May 2026).
strengths: A complete, mature SQL front end you don’t have to write: parser, validator with dialect and conformance settings (MySQL, Oracle, BigQuery, SQL Server lexical rules), and conversion to relational algebra
An optimizer built for extension: pluggable rules, cost models, statistics and planner engines, with hundreds of rules included
Federation through adapters: one query can join tables from different systems, with rules pushing filters, joins and aggregations down to each source
Proven by adoption: Hive, Flink, Druid, Dremio, Beam, Drill and many more rely on it, so its parser and planner are exercised by a lot of production workloads
limits: Java only: an engine written in C++ or Rust has to run a JVM beside it, or pass plans across a language boundary
Not a database: no storage or catalog, and its built-in `Enumerable` execution runs row by row over iterators, so heavy work has to be pushed into an engine
The library API moves: release notes open with a “Breaking Changes” list (1.42.0 renamed methods and changed how DDL nodes report their operands), so embedders must budget for upgrades

Planning costs time: the cost-based planner can search exhaustively, so systems stop early when the cost stops improving or split rules into phases and run some with the cheaper planner that doesn’t cost plans

sections.title: What Calcite gives you, and what it leaves out

items.name: SQL parser and validator
items.text: Standard SQL with sub-queries, window aggregates, `GROUPING SETS` and streaming extensions, checked against your schema. Lexical rules for Oracle (the default), MySQL, BigQuery, SQL Server and Java.

items.name: Relational algebra
items.text: The plan as a tree of operators, which you can also build directly in code. The 2014 proposal noted that Hive did just that, skipping Calcite’s SQL parser.

items.name: Optimizer
items.text: Rules, metadata providers (row counts, selectivity, cost) and two planner engines: cost-based (Volcano-style) and a rule-firing one that skips costing. Materialized-view rewriting and lattices on top.

items.name: Adapters
items.text: Make a source look like tables and push work into it: JDBC, Cassandra, MongoDB, Elasticsearch, Druid, Kafka, Redis, Arrow, files and Java objects.

items.name: JDBC driver
items.text: Built on Avatica, local or remote over JSON or Protobuf on HTTP, so tools can connect to a Calcite schema like any database.

items.name: Storage, execution at scale, catalog
items.text: You bring them: an engine such as Hive, Flink or Druid runs the optimized plan, and its own metastore supplies the tables.

story: Traditional databases bundled storage, execution, a parser, a planner and a catalog into one product. The Hadoop and NoSQL systems of the early 2010s split that stack apart, and most of them had fast storage and runtimes but no SQL and no real optimizer. As the 2014 incubator proposal put it, building a query planner is hard, so “many systems muddle along without a planner” until customers demand one. Julian Hyde, lead developer of the Mondrian OLAP engine, started Optiq as a reusable one. The first commits, in May 2012, imported source files from the Eigenbase project and added Optiq code that could parse and validate SQL but not yet plan.

Before it reached Apache, Optiq was already inside Apache Drill, Apache Hive and Cascading Lingual. It entered the Apache Incubator on 19 May 2014 with committers from Concurrent, Hortonworks, MapR and Salesforce, was renamed Calcite that September, and became a top-level Apache project on 22 October 2015. Hive was a key early user: as it moved from batch jobs toward interactive SQL, it needed a strong optimizer at its core and adopted Calcite for that. Flink, Storm, Druid and MapD were using it by 2018, and the project’s powered-by list now also names Dremio, Beam, Drill, Kylin and Feldera. A 2018 SIGMOD paper by Edmon Begoli, Jesús Camacho-Rodríguez, Julian Hyde, Michael Mior and Daniel Lemire described the architecture and why it spread.

choices.choice: Leave out storage, execution algorithms and the metadata store
choices.why: Those are what specialized systems do best and want to keep. Omitting them made Calcite a fit for mediating between applications and many data stores, and a base on which to build a new database: “just add data”.

choices.choice: The engine that runs an operator is just another trait
choices.why: Treating the calling convention like sort order or partitioning let one cost-based search decide where each part of a query runs, so a single plan can span MySQL, Splunk and Spark.

choices.choice: Two planner engines instead of one
choices.why: A Volcano-style cost-based planner finds good plans but can be slow; a second engine fires rules quickly without costing them. Offering both lets systems split optimization into phases and control planning time.
Most of the data systems it aimed at, especially in the Hadoop ecosystem, were written in Java or Scala, so a Java library could be embedded in them directly.
